blocks.text: Paul’s arrival in Jerusalem belongs to a larger journey. Paul’s letters identify a major collection for Jerusalem, while Acts recounts the travel and accompanying delegates without foregrounding the money itself. That difference is debated, so the chapter should not be read as explaining every purpose of the journey.

The decree repeated in verse 25 has significant textual variation. Some Western witnesses preserve a shorter, more moralized form, so readers should distinguish the familiar wording of the decree from conclusions about its precise purpose.

The brief notice that Philip’s four daughters prophesied is part of Acts’s selective portrayal of women as active participants in the movement—as disciples, prophets, hosts, patrons, teachers, workers, converts, and sufferers—while its narration still reflects patriarchal constraints.

The soldiers’ intervention stops the immediate beating but begins Paul’s custody. The following narrative develops this through hearings, legal claims, transfers, plots, governors, an appeal, travel, and confinement. It presents legal maneuvering amid restricted movement, without making every procedure an exact precedent or portraying imperial justice as consistently benevolent.
